claims.claim: The first Alpha Arena season (October-November 2025): Qwen3 Max won, DeepSeek was second, most models lost and GPT-5 finished last.
claims.evidence: Forklog reported the final balances: Qwen3 Max about 12,231 dollars, DeepSeek 10,489, Claude Sonnet 4.5 about 5,799, Gemini 2.5 Pro 5,445, Grok 4,208, GPT-5 4,126 (each model started with 10,000). Only two profited. The organizers said the capital was small and the period short, so it is not a statistical ranking.
claims.note: Remember it as the story of one season (n=1). The original source is Nof1; the agent read secondary coverage, not their page.

claims.claim: The ranking of language models in trading is not stable between seasons, and fewer than half the seasons are profitable.
claims.evidence: Season 1.5 (US stocks, around December 2025) was won by the "Mystery Model" (Grok 4.20, about +12% on average), with GPT-5.1 second and Gemini 3 third. GPT-5 was last in the first season, so the instability of the ranking is real. No source was found that computes a "share of profitable seasons", and there are only two seasons.
claims.note: The more accurate wording: in the two published seasons most models lost and the ranking changed. We drop the "fewer than half the seasons" figure unless there is a source.

claims.claim: Live academic benchmarks find that general model intelligence does not turn into trading skill, and risk management is weak.
claims.evidence: AI-Trader (arXiv 2512.10971) found that most agents have weak returns and weak risk control. TraderBench (12 models) found crypto strategies nearly static and the benefit of extended reasoning not measurable. Agent Market Arena found that the design of the framework matters more than the model.
claims.note: These are preprints and the agent read the abstracts only. We cite them by name and prefer them to news leaderboards.

claims.claim: A multi-stage crypto benchmark shows a backtest to paper to live gap, and traditional machine learning beats language agents on history.
claims.evidence: No paper was found showing that traditional machine learning beats language agents on crypto. What exists is "The Alpha Illusion" (arXiv 2605.16895): it says the published return of language agents is not evidence of readiness for operation, and it re-ran TradingAgents and QuantAgent for a year against buy and hold.
claims.note: We ask the author of the item for the exact paper title. Until then we cite Alpha Illusion for the narrower claim: a short in-sample backtest of language agents is not operating evidence.

claims.claim: The Sepp & Lucic (2026) paper "The Science and Practice of Trend-Following Systems" supports trend following on liquid contracts.
claims.evidence: The paper exists (arXiv 2607.19497): it classifies trend systems (European, American, TSMOM) and shows that trend is profitable when long-term autocorrelation is positive even with short-term reversal, and that all the systems are strongly correlated. The agent saw the abstract description only.
claims.note: The claims "the net depends on the lookback period" and "it dies on small timeframes after costs" were not verified from the paper. We read the PDF before quoting numbers. A 50/50 blend of trend + reversion (Setup4Alpha) is a hypothesis: what is published gives only a 0.32 correlation, with no CAGR, Sharpe, period or costs.

claims.claim: Donchian-55 (Turtle) on NQ: the profit factor of buys is high, and the profit factor of sells is far below 1.
claims.evidence: No source was found showing NQ buys and sells separately. The QuantifiedStrategies site was blocked by a bot check. The numbers it found are for other systems (monthly ETFs, or a 35% win rate and a 2.4 reward/risk with no clear instrument).
claims.note: We do not quote PF numbers. We do the buy/sell split ourselves on NQ with costs in the lab. The explanation of the long bias (an index that rises structurally) is reasonable but was not tested.

claims.claim: Mechanical SMC/ICT rules give a PF of about 1.2-1.5 after costs, and a full ICT bot can lose within a year (Puravida Edge 2026, Raw Edge).
claims.evidence: No trace of "Puravida Edge" or "Raw Edge" was found. The closest independent source: Mahadzva (2026, SSRN, not yet peer reviewed): six ICT/SMC rules on four forex pairs, and the abstract says "no evidence that ICT/SMC concepts work as taught", although the best holdout case gave a PF of 1.50 on 60 trades. Another survey found no rigorous test.
claims.note: The direction (a weak or absent edge) is supported, but we cannot trace the source of the 1.2-1.5 figure. We attribute it to Mahadzva or drop the names. SMC stays context only. The 78-92% win rates from vendors with no data: we ignore them.

claims.claim: A liquidity sweep / session reclaim gives a small edge (PF about 1.3) on large samples, not the 70-80% rates in the marketing.
claims.evidence: No independent source was found for PF 1.3. The figures that exist come from a vendor or a hobbyist (Backtrex, or one EA on a demo). Mahadzva found that three sweep rules showed continuation in 65 of 66 choices, the opposite of the reversal story.
claims.note: We treat "sweep then reversal" as unproven, and we test both reversal and continuation in the lab with costs. We drop "PF 1.3".

claims.claim: Order flow works as a gate at a level, but its evidence as a stand-alone system is weak.
claims.evidence: The academic support is for the price effect, not for a tradable profit: Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov found that short price changes are driven mainly by imbalance at the best bid and ask, with a linear relationship whose slope is inversely related to depth (50 NYSE stocks). No independent test with costs was found for footprint or absorption rules.
claims.note: Imbalance predicts the next move directly at the book level, but that does not prove a footprint rule is profitable after fees. We keep it as a recorded gate and measure it ourselves.

claims.claim: Session timing / Kill Zones improve results (for example PF +0.47).
claims.evidence: Volatility seasonality is documented: a EUR/USD study and an RBA bulletin (14 years of AUD) find the highest volatility in the London-New York overlap. But the +6.1 points of win rate and +0.47 PF from Kill Zones come only from Backtrex (a vendor). Older GARCH work on EUR/USD found the opposite (higher in Asian hours).
claims.note: Sessions as a volatility and liquidity filter are acceptable. "Kill Zones add an edge" is not proven. We use the exchange's local time because of daylight saving.

claims.claim: Coinbase for Agents lets AI assistants trade the user's account through MCP/CLI with spending limits.
claims.evidence: Launched June 11, 2026: an MCP server (ChatGPT and Claude) and a CLI (Claude Code and others). The user sets spending limits and there is an isolated wallet. Crypto spot and derivatives at launch, and US stocks later according to a report. No total volume has been announced; the only one published is for one week (September 14-21) with per-client shares.
claims.note: The Coinbase blog returned 403 to the agent, so the details come from research summaries and Decrypt. We do not quote a "total volume".

claims.claim: Robinhood launched Agentic Trading (a separate agent account, MCP, stocks only in the beta).
claims.evidence: Launched May 27, 2026 together with an agentic credit card. Agents connect to MCP servers and the money sits in a separate agent account; the user receives alerts and can pause or disconnect. Stocks only for now and the other tools "coming soon". One source says agents can execute stock trades without per-trade approval.
claims.note: This matches the minutes' point "a product, not performance evidence". The approval mode matters: Robinhood and Coinbase allow limited autonomy, not just an assistant.

claims.claim: IBKR, Webull, eToro and others offer agent/MCP integration (the minutes classify them as type C).
claims.evidence: Webull: an MCP server from April 2026, announced June 11, 2026, supporting ChatGPT, Claude and Grok and able to place and modify orders. IBKR: an official MCP integration (FOW, late July 2026), but two secondary sources say the AI prepares the trade and the client submits the order manually. eToro: weak sources only.
claims.note: We do not lump them into one approval pattern: Webull executes orders, IBKR does analysis and manual submission, eToro is unconfirmed.

claims.claim: SoFi's Composer turns ideas in English into rule strategies that are tested and deployed, with a community catalog.
claims.evidence: SoFi acquired Composer (terms undisclosed). The user describes an idea and the AI produces rules that are tested and deployed, and there are more than 2,000 community strategies. Composer continues as a standalone product.
claims.note: The product description is confirmed; there is no independent audit of the community strategies' returns, so the over-fitting warning stays.

claims.claim: Idea: forex price levels and stop-order clusters (Osler, the New York Fed) as an empirical basis for the "Levels" module.
claims.evidence: According to a survey: support and resistance levels published by 6 firms bounced 60.8% of the time versus 56.2% for random levels (1996-1998). And a study of 9,667 dealer orders found that stop orders cluster after round numbers. Rigorous support for levels is rare, and it fits with levels being the best family in our lab.
claims.note: The agent saw the numbers from a survey page, not from the PDF. The data is 1990s forex: we re-test on our assets. The 4.6-point difference is small.

claims.claim: Idea: protection against multiple testing in the lab: Deflated Sharpe, Probability of Backtest Overfitting and a t threshold above 3.
claims.evidence: Bailey and Lopez de Prado: the Deflated Sharpe corrects the selection bias across many attempts. Bailey and co-authors: PBO by combinatorially symmetric cross-validation (there is a CRAN package called pbo). Harvey, Liu and Zhu (2016): t above 3. The lab compares many families, so the more we try, the more false winners we find.
claims.note: We apply them to the lab's number of attempts (every school, timeframe and parameter). The Harvey-Liu-Zhu link was seen only through a survey. Our lab's gate (t > 3) is already close to this.

claims.claim: Idea: test the order flow gate with a tick-level backtester that simulates queue position and latency (the open-source hftbacktest).
claims.evidence: hftbacktest is an open-source Python/Rust framework that rebuilds the book from level 2 and 3 data and simulates tick by tick with queue position and order latency. It has a live bot for Binance Futures and Bybit, and some Rust parts are described as experimental.
claims.note: Useful only if we store real L2/L3 data; with candles alone it adds nothing. It complements the NautilusTrader mentioned in the minutes.

claims.claim: Idea: a "random baseline" column for every signal in the scanner, and the Alpha Illusion protocol for minimum reporting.
claims.evidence: A random simulation in the thortradecopier analysis: FVG gaps were visited 83.4% versus 83.5% for random levels, so a pattern must beat a random baseline after costs on unseen data. The Alpha Illusion paper proposes structural tests and a P1-P6 reporting protocol, and that language models act as an auditable information interface feeding separate risk and execution modules.
claims.note: The 83.4% versus 83.5% figure is the blog author's simulation, not peer reviewed. The random-baseline column is cheap and fits an honest lab.
